summary:
We built a health monitoring and incident response system for three-person crews on long space missions. H.E.R.B (Hypoxia Emergency Response Beta); small sensor board behind the astronaut’s ear uses red and infrared light to measure blood oxygen (SpO₂) and heart rate. A Raspberry Pi hub sends these readings to AEGIS; the helmet displays (HUDs) of both spacewalkers and to H.E.R.A (Hypoxia Emergency Response Assistant); a tablet used by a third crew member inside the spacecraft.

Spacesuits run at low pressure with 100% oxygen, so any leak can quickly cause hypoxia. This health monitoring system compares live readings with each astronaut’s pre-mission baseline. It raises an amber warning when SpO₂ stays more than three standard deviations below normal for 3 seconds, and a red critical alert at 5 seconds. Heart rate only counts as supporting evidence, so normal exertion doesn’t trigger false alarms. The HUDs alert both spacewalkers with visual and sound cues. Meanwhile, the tablet guides the onboard crew member through first aid with multiple-choice prompts and logs every incident.

Spacewalks average 0.26 injuries per EVA, and no current suit reliably prevents hypoxia. As missions head to the Moon and Mars, personalised real-time monitoring with guided response could help bring hypoxia deaths down to zero.
details:
PROBLEM STATEMENT 

How might we create a health monitoring system that can diagnose and guide incident resolution for acute work incidents during EVA missions, specifically hypoxia. 

With the ambitions to establish moon bases, commercial flights and a round trip to Mars, acute healthcare in space becomes imperative to a safe spaceflight. We understand there is work to be done in space, and as such we understand work incidents are an inevitability. 

Considering the design trade-off of lower suit pressure for more mobility, the suit is filled with 100% oxygen due to the low suit pressure. This is important because the body needs a specific minimum physical pressure for oxygen so that it may be pushed from the lungs into the bloodstream. 

As a result, this optimisation for suit mobility makes any oxygen leak fatal, putting the astronaut at an elevated risk of hypoxia.

Despite the small number of recorded cases in the history of spaceflight, we feel 1 hypoxia fatality is already 1 too many, and given the prospect of prolonged spaceflight arising from the direction of the space industry, we feel strongly about reducing the number of hypoxia fatalities on such flights to ZERO.

MVP SOLUTION

We created an interactive work incident response tool designed for 3-man space crews in prolonged space missions. There are 3 components to this product. Firstly H.E.R.B (Hypoxia Emergency Response Beta), a custom made hardware to sense SpO2 and heart rate through infrared rays and red light. Secondly, AEGIS is an astronaut helmet HUD developed for rapid intuitive display of incidents through visual and audio cues. Thirdly, H.E.R.A (Hypoxia Emergency Response Assistant) is an app developed for tablet use, that serves as a guide for first aid and incidents response entailing primarily hypoxia.

Using astronaut helmet HUDs, we use visual and auditory cues to alert the EVA astronaut buddy system of hypoxia incidents using SpO2 and heart rate readings measured against the astronauts biodata through custom hardware. A third crew member monitoring the EVA activity from within the spacecraft would have access to a tablet that reflects the real-time monitoring of astronauts on the EVA mission, synched with the readings of the astronaut helmet HUDs. 

The tablet, upon alerted to hypoxia status of an astronaut conducting EVAs, would administer instructions to this third crew member through a gamified system of multiple choice to deliver the proper care to the affected astronaut. 

POTENTIAL IMPACT

Spacewalks generate an incidence rate of 0.26 injuries per EVA and the market does not have reliable hypoxia preventive suits, the proposed solution will enhance EVA safety by enabling astronauts to recognise physiological abnormalities.

With further validation and hardware development, the concept could support future lunar exploration missions and other high-risk environments requiring continuous physiological monitoring.

The proposed system could improve EVA safety by enabling astronauts to recognise physiological abnormalities without repeatedly consulting external monitoring interfaces.

PRODUCT FLOW

In the event of a Hypoxia Incident:

  1. Hardware primarily detects abnormal SpO2 and heart rate readings more than 2-3 standard deviations away for X amount of seconds from the astronaut’s biodata mean recorded pre-launch.
  2. The HUD display on the astronaut helmet alerts the EVA astronaut buddy system of a hypoxia incident through visual and audio cues.
  3. The tablet in the spacecraft is alerted of the hypoxia incident and provides clear instructions to the user on how to navigate incident resolution. 

NOTABLE DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

  • Auditory cues for warnings are included as firstly, retinal function decreases significantly for individuals affected by hypoxia, and secondly, other personnel cannot be expected to pay 100% attention to visual displays the whole time. 
  • We used astronaut HUDs as we understand that a buddy is always the first responder in the event of hypoxia and this UI location serves as the most obvious for a fast response. This feature was chosen with the understanding most EVA missions happen in a buddy system.
  • The tablet design was chosen given iPads are commonplace on the ISS, and the gamified first aid feature does respond to touchscreen.
  • We chose obvious simplistic cues/instructions for MCQ and HUD, with simple infographics accompanying the MCQs. The reason for this was to keep instructions as clear as possible given the immediacy of a hypoxia incident, 
  • Given the implied relationship from literature research between microgravity and hemodynamics, and how this might affect SpO2 and heart rate. We designed a rule based system to flag a hypoxia attack based on the astronaut’s individual biodata measured shortly prior to the EVA through a custom built sensor, instead of relying solely on a dataset from pre-launch
  • Placement of UI components for HUD for at the top of the view at baseline, and only warnings or alerts would mildly obstruct the astronauts view so as to prompt a timely response.

HARDWARE (H.E.R.B)

OVERALL DEVICE: Custom PCB - An embedded system to prevent hypoxia in astronauts in EVA suits. It is embedded to keep the entire device as small as possible since the sensor will be positioned behind the ear, as it is the most accurate place to take both BPM and SP02 measurements, key indicators of potential hypoxia. It will be integrated into the headgear of the astronaut. The embedded system is incredibly energy-efficient and will be able to perform its single task of data acquisition well and reliably for long periods of time. 

SENSOR: IR + Red Light - This is the device that measures the body for specific vitals: BPM and SP02. This is to monitor the astronaut to prevent hypoxia. It samples every 6 seconds continuously (1 second to sample, then 5 sec delay; this 6-second process is then repeated continuously, and the previous 15 cycles of sampling are retained, with anything older being erased to save on storage).
It uses the IR and Red Light to see how much of each is absorbed, given how IR is absorbed by Oxyhemoglobin (red, oxygenated blood cells) and Red Light is absorbed by deoxyhemoglobin, and returns the corresponding raw values.

MCU: ESP32-WROOM - Brain that computes the raw data into understandable, refined numbers reflecting real SP02 and BPM numbers. Then it transmits via Bluetooth to the Brain (RP)

BRAIN: Raspberry Pi (RP) - The main communicator to the 2 HUDs and Tablet. It takes the refined data and updates all of them, triggering any necessary warnings on each device

DISPLAY: Projector - This displays the HUD. This is for the astronauts’ indicator of their health and vitals LIVE. Displays a warning when their body experiences dangerous vitals based on the previous 15 samples of their live data against their recorded nominal data in the NASA Database. It is controlled by the RP and listens via Bluetooth. 

ANCHOR: Tablet - For the astronaut onboard the ship. This is the master control where he can monitor any astronaut outside on a spacewalk and assist them with what to do in order to save the astronaut. It is controlled by the RP and listens via Bluetooth.
Worth noting: 

  • ESP32 is equipped with long-range Bluetooth capabilities. Bluetooth is a concept that has been validated for space. 
  • Our device will be a single micro PCB that is able to do all the data acquisition, data processing, and long-distance transmission.

ASTRONAUT HELMET HUD (AEGIS)

The HUD places physiological readings along the edges of the astronaut’s foveal vision. 

PHYSIOLOGICAL MONITORING:

The system monitors four key parameters:

  • Oxygen saturation (SpO₂)
  • Heart rate
  • Breathing rate
  • Oxygen reserve

Mission time and elapsed EVA duration, as well as the buddy's geolocation are also displayed.

PERSONALISED ANOMALY DETECTION:

A potential abnormality is identified when SpO₂ falls more than three standard deviations below the baseline mean.

To reduce false alarms, the system requires the abnormality to persist before escalating:

  • Normal: No sustained abnormality detected.
  • Warning (Amber): Abnormal SpO₂ persists for 3 seconds.
  • Critical (Red): Abnormal SpO₂ persists for 5 seconds in total.

Heart rate acts as supporting evidence rather than an independent alert trigger. This helps prevent elevated heart rate caused by normal physical exertion from being incorrectly classified as an emergency. 

When an alert occurs, the interface obstructs the astronaut’s view with a prominent central message.

  • Amber indicates a warning.
  • Red indicates a critical condition.
  • Relevant physiological measurements are highlighted to help astronauts identify the source of the alert.

The buddy's geolocation feature will highlight in red if he is experiencing hypoxia, or yellow if he is experiencing a substantial drop in SpO2.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES:

In the actual application the HUD syncs with the custom sensor data.

The HUD uses React to render an interactive, browser-based helmet HUD with physiological telemetry.

The system incorporates configurable physiological baselines, statistical anomaly detection, and duration-based alert thresholds to distinguish potential oxygen deprivation from normal physical exertion. The HUD is deployed on Vercel, to prove its functionality in a vacuum, using simulated time series data and can be accessed here: https://astronaut-eva-hud.vercel.app/


TABLET UI (H.E.R.A)

OVERALL FUNCTION: The tablet UI is to be used by a third party on the spacecraft to monitor the vitals of the 2 astronauts conducting the EVA. It primarily senses SpO2 and heart rate among other important values, and alerts the user if the readings deviates from the mean significantly for 3-5 seconds and it also has a gamified first aid system in the event of hypoxia and/or decompression sickness. The incident and notable incident responses are recorded into the Logs tab. It should be noted the time gap between the initial drop and the alert, as well as the standard deviation of vitals away from the biodata mean can be modified to be specific to different extents of suit leaks. 

The gamified first aid system features a multiple choice / complete all objectives style UI that is meant to guide the user on how to measure vitals, conduct first aid, and incident resolution for hypoxia / decompression sickness incidents. 

BACKEND: The backend is a Python FastAPI server, run by Uvicorn, that holds the mission state and runs the hypoxia detector once a second on each crewmember's readings. It pushes every update to the screen over a WebSocket, and it serves the response protocols (JSON decision trees), the NASA DCS model and the event log. In the demo build the readings come from the recorded NASA and analog data; in the hardware build they come from the ESP32 + MAX30102 sensors. 

FRONTEND: The frontend is a React 18 + TypeScript app built with Vite, which draws its charts and illustrations as hand-written SVG. It plays alerts with the browser's built-in sound and speech, and installs on the iPad as an offline app that runs full screen. 

There's also a browser-only build hosted on Vercel, which runs the same detector in TypeScript without a server, using time series simulated data to prove its functionality in a vacuum and it can be accessed over here: https://crew-health-tablet.vercel.app


Here is a guide on how to use the app:

  1. The first 10 seconds is used to measure a pre-EVA baseline for astronaut biodata. (Actual operation will feature 4min measurement times, the demo pre-EVA measurement is 10sec for the sake of time)
  2. At the 20sec mark, a hypoxia alert for EV1 will be triggered and you get to play the MCQ!
  3. The second and third tabs are for checking hypoxia and decompression sickness manually.
dataRefs: NASA crew physiology: ECG, heart rate, HRV and breathing from 18 pilots, with startle events
NASA hypoxia evidence report (2015): hypoxia symptoms, countermeasures, suit and cabin atmospheres
NASA decompression sickness treatment model (TP-2014-218561): recovery odds by pressure and O₂
NASA spacewalk log, US and Russia (1965–2013): crew, duration and suit incidents
NASA hypoxia risk graph: causes, countermeasures and outcomes of hypoxia
projectRefs: Harespod (analog, non-NASA): SpO₂, heart rate and breathing in an altitude chamber, 1,500–4,000+ m
